status: Fully sovereign duchy, personal union with Brandenburg
summary: The Treaty of Oliva ended Polish feudal overlordship, making the Hohenzollern Duchy of Prussia fully sovereign - the springboard for the proclamation of the Kingdom of Prussia in 1701.

name: Margraviate of Brandenburg
summary: Core Mark Brandenburg (Altmark, Mittelmark, Prignitz, Uckermark, Neumark) held first by Wittelsbach then Luxembourg margraves before the Hohenzollern acquisition.

name: Electorate of Brandenburg (without Neumark)
status: Imperial electorate with alienated eastern territory
summary: The historical era (covering late Luxembourg rule and early Hohenzollern acquisition) when the Neumark was pawned to the Teutonic Order, leaving core Brandenburg without its easternmost territory until its redemption in 1454-1455.

name: Electorate of Brandenburg (Hohenzollern)
summary: Emperor Sigismund enfeoffed Frederick of Hohenzollern with Brandenburg in 1415, founding the dynasty that would later build Prussia; territorial extent stayed close to the earlier Mark.

name: County of Ravensberg
status: Electorate in personal union with Ducal Prussia and the Rhenish duchies
summary: In 1618 the Hohenzollerns inherited Ducal Prussia, and from 1614 they held Cleves-Mark-Ravensberg in the Rhineland, creating a scattered composite state; core Brandenburg borders shown here (Prussia's own extent given separately).

name: County of Mark
status: Electorate in personal union with Ducal Prussia and the Rhenish duchies
summary: In 1618 the Hohenzollerns inherited Ducal Prussia, and from 1614 they held Cleves-Mark-Ravensberg in the Rhineland, creating a scattered composite state; core Brandenburg borders shown here (Prussia's own extent given separately).

name: Duchy of Cleves
status: Electorate in personal union with Ducal Prussia and the Rhenish duchies
summary: In 1618 the Hohenzollerns inherited Ducal Prussia, and from 1614 they held Cleves-Mark-Ravensberg in the Rhineland, creating a scattered composite state; core Brandenburg borders shown here (Prussia's own extent given separately).

name: Brandenburg (in union with Prussia & Cleves-Mark)
status: Electorate in personal union with Ducal Prussia and the Rhenish duchies
summary: In 1618 the Hohenzollerns inherited Ducal Prussia, and from 1614 they held Cleves-Mark-Ravensberg in the Rhineland, creating a scattered composite state; core Brandenburg borders shown here (Prussia's own extent given separately).

name: Pomerania
summary: The Peace of Westphalia awarded Brandenburg Farther Pomerania (Sweden kept Western Pomerania with Stettin) plus the secularized bishoprics of Kammin, Halberstadt and Minden.

name: Bishopric of Minden
summary: The Peace of Westphalia awarded Brandenburg Farther Pomerania (Sweden kept Western Pomerania with Stettin) plus the secularized bishoprics of Kammin, Halberstadt and Minden.

name: Bishopric of Halberstadt
summary: The Peace of Westphalia awarded Brandenburg Farther Pomerania (Sweden kept Western Pomerania with Stettin) plus the secularized bishoprics of Kammin, Halberstadt and Minden.

name: Brandenburg (post-Westphalia, +Farther Pomerania)
summary: The Peace of Westphalia awarded Brandenburg Farther Pomerania (Sweden kept Western Pomerania with Stettin) plus the secularized bishoprics of Kammin, Halberstadt and Minden.

name: Ducy of Mahdeburg
summary: After the Treaty of Oliva freed Prussia from Polish suzerainty, Brandenburg absorbed Magdeburg (1680) and stood as the core of a scattered but powerful realm - crowned as the Kingdom of Prussia in 1701 (Ducal Prussia's own extent given separately).

name: Brandenburg-Prussia (sovereign composite state)
summary: After the Treaty of Oliva freed Prussia from Polish suzerainty, Brandenburg absorbed Magdeburg (1680) and stood as the core of a scattered but powerful realm - crowned as the Kingdom of Prussia in 1701 (Ducal Prussia's own extent given separately).

name: Duchy of Saxe-Wittenberg
summary: The small Ascanian electoral duchy centred on Wittenberg held the Saxon electoral title until the dynasty died out in 1422.

name: Electorate of Saxony (Wettin, unified)
summary: Emperor Sigismund transferred the vacant Saxon electoral title to Frederick the Warlike, Margrave of Meissen, uniting Meissen, Thuringia and Wittenberg under Wettin rule.

name: Ernestine Saxony (Electoral line)
summary: The Treaty of Leipzig split Wettin lands between two brothers; the elder Ernestine line kept the electoral title along with Thuringia and Wittenberg.

name: Albertine Saxony (Ducal line)
summary: The younger Albertine branch received Meissen and Dresden without the electoral dignity, until Duke Maurice flipped the title in the Schmalkaldic War.

name: Lusatia
summary: Acquired by the Electorate of Saxony via the 1635 Peace of Prague, integrating Upper and Lower Lusatia into Saxon rule under the House of Wettin.

name: Electorate of Saxony (Albertine, reunified)
summary: After the Schmalkaldic War, Maurice of Saxony was rewarded with the electoral title and most Ernestine lands, permanently fixing Dresden as the seat of a reunified Electorate of Saxony.

name: Duchy of Bavaria (partitioned)
summary: Bavaria was split among competing Wittelsbach lines (Munich, Landshut, Ingolstadt, Straubing) for over a century; overall Bavarian territory shown combined here.

name: Duchy of Bavaria (reunified)
summary: The Landshut War of Succession (1503-1505) reunited nearly all Bavarian lands under the Munich line of the Wittelsbachs.

name: Electorate of Bavaria (+Upper Palatinate)
summary: Duke Maximilian I was granted the electoral title in 1623 for his role in the Thirty Years' War, and the Upper Palatinate was transferred to Bavaria, confirmed at the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.

name: Kingdom of Denmark
summary: Under Valdemar IV, Denmark reconsolidated after decades of pawned territory, retaining Jutland, the Danish islands and Scania (Skåne) on the eastern side of the Sound.

name: Kalmar Union (Denmark-Norway-Sweden)
summary: Margaret I united Denmark, Norway and Sweden (with Finland) under a single crown; Denmark provided the union's dominant partner and monarch.

name: Denmark-Norway
summary: After Gustav Vasa led Sweden out of the Kalmar Union, Denmark retained Norway plus Scania, Halland, Blekinge and Bohuslän on the eastern Sound shore - the union's core minus Sweden-Finland.

name: Denmark-Norway (post-Roskilde)
summary: The Treaties of Roskilde and Copenhagen forced Denmark to cede Scania, Halland, Blekinge and Bohuslän to Sweden, permanently shifting the Sound border and shrinking the kingdom to Jutland, the Danish isles and Norway.

name: Kingdom of Sweden (with Finland)
summary: Sweden's medieval core included Finland; it entered the Kalmar Union with Denmark and Norway in 1397, remaining the union's junior, often restless, partner.

name: Kingdom of Sweden (independent)
summary: Gustav Vasa led Sweden's secession from the Kalmar Union in 1523, restoring full independence over the same Sweden-Finland core before the Baltic and German expansions began.

name: Swedish Estonia (Baltic dominion)
summary: Tallinn and the Estonian nobility submitted to Sweden during the Livonian War in 1561, beginning a Baltic overseas empire later expanded with Livonia (1629) and Ingria (1617/1629).

name: Swedish Pomerania & Bremen-Verden
status: Imperial fiefs held by the Swedish crown
summary: The Peace of Westphalia gave Sweden Western Pomerania (with Stettin and Wismar) plus the secularized bishoprics of Bremen and Verden, making Sweden a permanent power inside the Holy Roman Empire.

name: Kingdom of Sweden (post-Roskilde, imperial peak)
status: Kingdom, at the height of the Swedish Empire
summary: The Treaties of Roskilde and Copenhagen (1658-1660) added Scania, Halland, Blekinge and Bohuslän from Denmark, giving Sweden its natural southern border and, with the Baltic and German dominions, the largest extent of the Swedish Empire.

name: Kingdom of England (with Wales & Pale of Ireland)
summary: The stable home-island core of the English crown - England, conquered Wales, and the Pale around Dublin in Ireland - which changed little while England's continental holdings rose and fell during this period.

name: English Gascony
summary: By 1352 English France was reduced to a coastal strip of Gascony around Bordeaux, plus the newly captured fortress of Calais (1347), the last remnants of the Angevin empire.

name: English Aquitaine (Treaty of Brétigny)
status: Sovereign principality of the English crown
summary: The Treaty of Brétigny gave Edward III full sovereignty over a vastly enlarged Aquitaine (Gascony, Poitou, Limousin, Perigord, Quercy), plus Calais and Ponthieu in the north, at the height of England's continental power before Charles V's reconquests.

name: Lancastrian France (Treaty of Troyes)
summary: The Treaty of Troyes recognized Henry V as heir to the French throne, briefly uniting Normandy, Paris and Aquitaine under English control before the tide turned after Joan of Arc's campaigns; England lost all of it by 1453 except Calais.

name: Pale of Calais
status: Fortified enclave, last English holding in France
summary: After the Hundred Years' War ended in 1453, England's continental possessions were reduced to the fortified Pale of Calais, held until its loss to France in 1558.

name: England, Wales, Ireland & Scotland (Union of the Crowns)
status: Personal union of separate kingdoms under one monarch
summary: James VI of Scotland's accession as James I of England in 1603 united the English and Scottish crowns in one person while keeping separate parliaments and legal systems, until the Acts of Union merged them into Great Britain in 1707.

name: Timurid Empire (Transoxiana core)
status: Emerging empire, nominal Chagatayid khans as figureheads
summary: Timur seized power in Transoxiana in 1370, ruling in the name of puppet Chagatayid khans while building the military base (Samarkand, Bukhara, Fergana) from which he would launch decades of conquest.

name: Timurid Empire (+Khwarezm & Khorasan)
summary: Timur absorbed Khwarezm and then Khorasan, capturing Herat in 1381 and extinguishing the Kartid dynasty, extending his rule from Transoxiana deep into eastern Persia.

name: Timurid Empire (+Persia, Fars & Azerbaijan)
summary: The Three-Year Campaign (1386-1388) brought Fars, Isfahan, Azerbaijan and Georgia under Timurid rule, extending the empire from Central Asia to the Caucasus and the Persian Gulf.

name: Timurid Empire (+Mesopotamia & the Caucasus)
summary: The Five-Year Campaign (1392-1396) added Baghdad, Mosul and Basra along with a firmer grip on Georgia, Shirvan and Derbent; Timur also raided deep into the Golden Horde and, in 1398, sacked Delhi (not permanently annexed).

name: Timurid Empire (peak extent)
summary: The Seven-Year Campaign (1399-1404) brought Syria (Aleppo, Damascus sacked 1400-1401) and, after crushing the Ottomans at Ankara in 1402, eastern Anatolia under Timurid control - the empire's maximum extent at Timur's death in 1405, stretching from the Aegean approaches to the borders of China.

name: Timurid Empire (Shah Rukh's realm)
status: Empire, capital moved from Samarkand to Herat
held: 1409-1469 (this extent, spanning Shah Rukh and Abu Sa'id)
summary: After a succession war, Shah Rukh reunited Khorasan, Transoxiana and most of Persia, but permanently lost Iraq, Syria and Anatolia to the Ottomans, Qara Qoyunlu and local dynasties; this core held broadly stable through Ulugh Beg and Abu Sa'id's reigns.

name: Timurid Empire (reduced to Khorasan & Transoxiana)
summary: Abu Sa'id's death fighting the Aq Qoyunlu at the Battle of Qarabagh (1469) cost the Timurids the rest of western and southern Persia (Fars, Isfahan, Kerman); under Sultan Husayn Bayqara the dynasty held only Khorasan and Transoxiana, its cultural high point under diminished borders.

name: Timurid Empire (Khorasan remnant)
summary: Muhammad Shaybani Khan's Uzbeks captured Samarkand and Bukhara in 1500, ending Timurid rule in Transoxiana; Sultan Husayn Bayqara held only Khorasan from Herat until his death in 1506, after which the Uzbeks took Herat in 1507, ending Timurid rule in Central Asia (Babur, a Timurid prince, would found the Mughal Empire in India in 1526).

name: Cyprus
summary: A vital eastern Mediterranean Venetian colony acquired in 1489 and held until its conquest by the Ottoman Empire in 1571.

name: Crete
summary: A fiercely contested Venetian maritime stronghold governed from 1204 until its fall to the Ottomans in 1669.

name: Cyprus
summary: Conquered from Venice.

name: Crete
summary: Conquered after the Siege of Candia.
